title: Believer 'does not work' means lacks law's perfect obedience—not empties of pious acts
source_text: XXXVII. Proinde juxta Paulum, per legem, sive opera nemo justificatur, nisi qui nullius est transgressionis reus, quique plane isti clausulae satisfecit, Qui fecerit ea homo vivet in eis. Illi vero qui credit in eum qui justificat impium, Deus justitiam sine operibus imputat, quoniam Deus illum pro justo habet, etiamsi non sit defunctus operibus quae lex exigit ad justificationem. Et similiter, quum credentem & operantem opponit Apostolus, docetque Deum justificare non operantem, sed credentem, per operantem intelligit illum qui opera lege praescripta sic praestitit, ut gratia opus non habeat, sed debeatur illi ex justitia merces: sicuti videre est cap. 4. epist. ad Rom. Ei qui operatur, inquit, merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito. Ei vero qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam. Ubi, quum dicit Apostolus non operari eum qui credit, manifestum est eum dicere nolle, quod qui credit sit bonis omnibus operibus vacuus. Nam in eo qui viva & salutari fide credit, necessario multa bona opera reperiuntur, qualia sunt, dolor de peccatis admissis, & anteactae vitae detestatio, votum & studium vitae melioris, veniae spes, & fiducia in Deum, denique & timor, & amor, & pia nominis ejus invocatio. Sed dicitur non operari qui credit, quoniam non praestat opera juxta legem ad vitam obtinendam necessaria. Ac quamvis fidem ejus multa pia & sancta opera comitentur, Deus tamen, ut loquitur Apostolus, justitiam illi imputat sine operibus, quoniam caret operibus legis; id est, perfecta illa & exacta obedientia, sine qua lex nullum justum pronunciat.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore according to Paul no one is justified through the law or works except the one guilty of no transgression who has fully satisfied that clause, The person who does them shall live by them. But to the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, God imputes righteousness without works, because God holds him as just even if he has not discharged the works the law requires for justification. And likewise, when the Apostle opposes the believer and the worker and teaches that God justifies not the one who works but the one who believes, by the one who works he means the one who so performed the works prescribed by the law that he has no need of grace, but wages are due him from justice—as is seen in Romans 4. To the one who works, he says, wages are not imputed from grace but from debt. But to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for righteousness. Where, when the Apostle says that the one who believes does not work, it is clear he does not mean that the believer is empty of all good works. For in the one who believes with living and saving faith many good works are necessarily found—such as sorrow for sins committed and detestation of former life, vow and pursuit of a better life, hope of pardon and trust in God, and finally fear and love and pious invocation of his name. But the one who believes is said not to work because he does not perform the works necessary according to the law for obtaining life. And although many pious and holy works accompany his faith, God nevertheless, as the Apostle speaks, imputes righteousness to him without works, because he lacks the works of the law—that is, that perfect and exact obedience without which the law pronounces no one just.
pass_b_english: Rom 4 'does not work' = lacks law's perfect wage-earning obedience—not lacks pious acts.
Living faith necessarily has sorrow, trust, love, prayer; God still imputes apart from legal perfection.

lemmas.gloss: lacks the works of the law

choices.why: Not legal-covenant worker; still has gospel fruits.
